Corven Spark Program: Week 2 Progress Report
Project: Corven, a browser-based IDE for building on CKB and Fiber Network
Reporting period: Week 2 (9–15 November 2026)
Reported: 15 November 2026
Project website: https://corvanide.space/
Status: On track, with one change to the session order (section 4)
1. Overview
Week 2 was the first full week after the committee’s approval. I used it to stabilize the platform and secure the infrastructure the remaining community sessions depend on. The work fell into two areas:
Renewing the hosting service so the public deployment stays online for the project period.
Preparing a stable version of Corven for the in-person sessions.
2. Activities Completed
2.1 Hosting service renewed
The hosting service behind the public instance at corvanide.space was recharged. This addresses the concern raised in the proposal review, when the earlier deployment was offline to save costs. The hosting covers the workspaces, devnets and Fiber nodes that participants will use in the sessions.
This was paid from the first installment (see section 5).
2.2 Corven updated to a stable version
The aim was for participants to be able to open a workspace, start a devnet and deploy a contract template reliably. The stable version is complete and is being deployed to the public instance ahead of the Thika session. It includes:
Guest mode. Participants can try Corven without signing up. The landing page’s “Open IDE” button takes them straight to the dashboard with a guest session. Guest workspaces are temporary and are deleted 24 hours after they were last used. If a guest connects a wallet or signs in, Corven asks which of their workspaces to keep. This removes the sign-up step from the start of each lab.
Workspace reliability fixes. A code reorganisation had dropped 18 API endpoints the IDE depends on, including the workspace status check, file saving and renaming, build, test, stop and the devnet controls. Opening a workspace failed with “Workspace not found”. I restored all of them and fixed two problems that stopped the API gateway from starting. Creating, starting and opening a workspace now works end to end.
A familiar IDE layout and a simpler dashboard. The workspace now follows the VS Code layout most developers already know: an activity bar, a file explorer, editor tabs that keep unsaved changes, a terminal panel and a status bar. I fixed a bug that stopped the editor from scrolling. The dashboard now shows only real workspace data and actions; placeholder statistics and panels that weren’t backed by live data were removed.
2.3 Thika session venue secured
The MKU Innovation Hub in Thika is confirmed for 19 November 2026. This was one of the two remaining in-person sessions in the proposal.
3. Progress Against Deliverables
#
Deliverable
Status at end of Week 2
1
Fiber playground
Three-node Fiber work (fnn v0.9.1) continues on the stable base. Packaging into the IDE and the recorded end-to-end verification are still pending.
2
Fiber starter templates
Not started. Follows the playground.
3
Getting-started guide
Not started. Will be updated using Thika session findings.
4
Open-source repository
Contribution readiness (license, docs, contribution guidelines) still to be addressed.
5
Stable public deployment
Hosting renewed. Stable version complete (guest mode, workspace reliability fixes, new IDE layout) and being deployed to corvanide.space. The 15–20 concurrent workspace load test and uptime monitoring are still pending.
6
Three community sessions
Session 1 (Kisumu, remote) completed. Thika confirmed for 19 Nov. Nairobi pending a host space.
7
User testing report
Structured attendance and survey collection will run at Thika.
8
Demo video
Planned for Week 5.
9
Final completion report
Planned for Week 5, with the line-item spending breakdown.
4. Change to the Session Plan
The proposal scheduled Nairobi before Thika. The Thika venue is now confirmed, while a suitable host space for the Nairobi session has not yet been secured. To avoid delaying the testing programme, the order is now:
Session
Original plan
Updated plan
Session 1
Kisumu (remote)
Completed, unchanged
Session 2
Nairobi
Thika, MKU Innovation Hub, 19 Nov 2026
Session 3
Thika
Nairobi, date to be confirmed once a host space is secured
What stays the same: the three-hour session format, the labs (CKB and Fiber), the feedback instruments, the participation targets (more than 40 participants in total, 70% Lab A completion, 50% Lab B completion, 80% survey response), the budget lines for each session, and the Week 5 completion target.
Because Thika is now the first in-person session, the Fiber playground may be less complete for it than it would have been for Nairobi. If Fiber isn’t fully integrated by 19 Nov, Lab B at Thika will use the most complete version available. The proposal allows for this (“progressing to multi-hop payments as the implementation becomes available”), and I will report exactly what participants could and could not do.
5. Funds Usage
The 20% first installment (104 USD, 89,041 CKB) was received and confirmed on the thread. It was used to pay for part of the hosting services under the “Cloud hosting and deployment” line of the approved budget (220 USD).
6. Risks and Open Items
Nairobi host space: Not yet secured. This is the main scheduling risk for Session 3. I am pursuing options and will confirm the date and host space on this thread as soon as they are settled.
Fiber playground timeline: Integration and verification are the largest remaining technical items. Thika is the first in-person test of whatever is ready.
Load and capacity: Each running workspace uses about 3 GB of memory. In development, the Docker host slowed noticeably with only a few workspaces running. The 15–20 concurrent workspace test is scheduled for the coming week, and its results will decide the server size and the per-session workspace limit for Thika. Results will be published.
Automated testing: The stable version was verified by hand. The end-to-end test suite still needs updating for the new IDE layout and dashboard before it can run against the release.
Remaining hosting: The first installment covered hosting only in part. Hosting for the rest of the project period depends on the remaining installments.
7. Priorities for Week 3 (16–22 November)
Complete the deployment of the stable version to corvanide.space and confirm the full workflow on the public instance: open a workspace as a guest, start a devnet, deploy a contract template.
Finalize preparation for the Thika session: participant instructions, baseline and post-session survey forms, bug-log template and attendance log.
Run and publish the load test for 15–20 concurrent workspaces, and set up uptime monitoring.
Hold and document the Thika session on 19 November, with attendance, lab completion and survey data.
Continue integrating the Fiber playground into the IDE.
Secure a host space for the Nairobi session and confirm its date.
Fix issues reported at Thika and prepare the first part of the user testing report.
8. Next Update
The next written update will be posted on Sunday, 22 November, and will include the Thika session results.
Submitted by: Jimleston Osoi
Project: Corven IDE, Spark Program Proposal

topics.title: Spark Program | ShareCut: referral payouts for small shops over Fiber (testnet)

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | ShareCut: referral payouts for small shops over Fiber (testnet)
recent_posts.author: abdul
recent_posts.content_text:
1. Project Overview
Small shops in Lagos get most new customers by word of mouth, but they rarely track it or pay the people who bring customers in. ShareCut gives each promoter a personal link or QR code. When a customer they referred pays through Fiber, the promoter’s agreed cut is paid automatically and both payments appear on a public receipts page.
ShareCut builds on an existing Fiber checkout and adds three things: referral attribution, an automatic payout service, and public receipts. It runs on testnet only, takes 6 weeks, and ends with a pilot in at least 2 real shops.
2. Team Profile
Name: Abdul (solo applicant)
Location: Lagos, Nigeria (student at the University of Lagos)
Contact: Discord olagoldhackxx, email aileruenterprise@gmail.com
GitHub: Olagold-hackxx (Abdulqoyyum Aileru) · GitHub
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/abdulqoyyum-aileru-017b75253
Project repo: GitHub - Olagold-hackxx/sharecut: Referral payouts for small shops over CKB Fiber (testnet). Spark Program project. · GitHub
I’m a software engineer with about 3 years of experience. At Go Digital Africa I was a Senior Software Engineer, where I led SNBS and co-led Linkly. I’ve also worked on LLM evaluation at Celsius, integrated Paystack payments, and designed a Stellar/Soroban USDC escrow dApp for a bounty. I write Rust and TypeScript.
I’m new to CKB and Fiber. Week 1 of this plan is set aside for running a Fiber node on testnet and learning the tooling.
Why I want to build this:
Most of what I’ve built so far has been payments: Paystack integrations at work, and an escrow app on Stellar. The problem I keep running into, though, isn’t paying. It’s getting customers. Small businesses around me in Lagos live on word of mouth, and the people who bring in customers usually get nothing, or a “thank you, I’ll sort you out later” that never comes. I want to see whether paying them automatically, per sale, changes anything. Fiber is a good place to try it because tiny payments are its whole point, and Spark lets me test it small and in public instead of guessing. If the pilot shows shops don’t care, I’ll say so.
3. Project Background
The shops I have in mind are the ordinary ones near campus and in the markets: provisions, food, printing, phone accessories. Their marketing is mostly WhatsApp statuses and people telling their friends. When someone does bring in a customer, any reward is informal (cash, a discount, airtime), and nobody writes it down.
I haven’t measured any of this yet. Before the pilot I’ll talk to at least 3 owners and post what they actually said in the first weekly update, including if it contradicts this section.
The problem is small but common. Word of mouth works, but nobody records who sent whom, so promoters are paid unevenly or not at all, and owners can’t tell which promoters actually bring sales.
4. Solution
The shop owner creates a promoter link or QR code for each promoter and sets their cut (for example 5%).
A customer opens the link and pays a Fiber invoice at checkout.
When the payment settles, ShareCut pays the promoter’s cut from the shop’s node.
Both the sale and the payout appear on a public receipts page with their payment hashes.
Why Fiber, honestly: in Nigeria, bank apps like OPay and Moniepoint already make transfers cheap and instant, so cost isn’t the argument. Fiber helps in three ways. Payouts are automatic and tied to each sale. Very small amounts per sale are practical. And a promoter only needs a Fiber invoice, not bank details. The weak spot is that today this is harder for a non-crypto shop than cash, and it’s testnet only. The pilot is meant to test whether shops care anyway.
5. Technical Approach
Reused:
FNN (Fiber Network Node), GitHub - nervosnetwork/fiber: A scalable, privacy-by-default payment & swap network · GitHub, on testnet
An existing Fiber checkout with invoices and webhooks: FiberFlow, GitHub - Ticoworld/fiberflow · GitHub. I haven’t tested it yet; week 1 confirms whether its payment events give me what I need. I’ll also reach out to its author.
A hosted-node pattern for people who can’t run their own node, as Fiber Link did for tipping
New:
Referral attribution: each promoter link carries an ID; the invoice is tagged with it.
Payout service (Rust): on a settled-payment event, it pays the promoter’s cut, at most once per sale (tracked by payment hash).
Public receipts page: each sale with its matching payout and payment hashes, readable without a wallet.
A simple shop dashboard to create promoter links and see totals.
The node runs on a small VPS. Each payout is keyed to the sale’s payment hash and recorded before it’s sent, so a repeated event finds the record and stops. If the checkout’s events don’t give me what I need, I’ll poll the node for settled invoices instead. It’s slower, but simpler.
6. To-Do List (6 weeks, about 10 hours a week)
Week
Work
Output
1
Run FNN on testnet, open channels, test the checkout’s payment events
Node ID, first test payment hash, short notes on what worked
2
Promoter links and invoice tagging
Demo: two promoter links, two tagged test payments
3
Payout service with pay-at-most-once
Payout hashes; a test showing a repeated event doesn’t pay twice
4
Public receipts page and shop dashboard
Public URL anyone can open
5
Pilot with real shops and promoters
Pilot log: shops, promoters, payments, problems
6
Fixes and final report
Final report with user feedback and setup guide
7. Required Funding & Breakdown
Requested: $900, paid in CKB.
Item
Basis
USD
Development and testing
54 hours × $15/hour
810
VPS for the testnet node
2 months, about $20/month
40
Pilot and feedback
Mobile data / airtime for shop owners and promoters
50
Total
900
If the committee approves less, I’ll cut the shop dashboard first and keep the receipts page and the pilot.
8. Deliverables + How to Verify
Deliverable
How to verify (no code review needed)
Public testnet demo
Open the URL, create a promoter link, pay with test funds, watch the payout appear
Public receipts page
Every sale listed next to its payout, with payment hashes
Pay-at-most-once
A recorded demo and a logged test where the same event is sent twice and only one payout appears
Open-source repo
Licence, README and a setup guide another developer can follow
Pilot report
Number of shops, promoters and payments, with owners’ feedback in their own words
9. Current State vs. Funded Work
Current state: an idea, plus a public repo with a README and MIT licence (GitHub - Olagold-hackxx/sharecut: Referral payouts for small shops over CKB Fiber (testnet). Spark Program project. · GitHub). No code yet. Everything in section 6 is funded work.
Limits: testnet only, with payouts in test CKB, not naira. The pilot uses a node I host for shops and promoters, which is custodial. Demand is unproven, and a “shops didn’t care” result will be reported honestly.
10. CKB Alignment
ShareCut isn’t another way to pay. It gives shops a reason to create Fiber payments, since each referred sale produces a payment and a payout. It sits on top of an existing checkout instead of rebuilding one, and it’s open source.
How it differs from nearby projects:
MeterNet sells Wi-Fi by the megabyte. ShareCut pays people for bringing customers.
Dular is about mobile payments and cashing out to fiat. ShareCut doesn’t touch fiat.
Fiber Link is tipping between users. ShareCut payouts are tied to a specific sale and set by the shop.

recent_posts.topic_title: A second post-quantum lock for CKB? ML-DSA beside SPHINCS+, checked and measured
recent_posts.author: LusoCryptoLabs
recent_posts.content_text:
What each signature rests on, and what that safety costs1600×900 80.3 KB
This is a study and a prototype, on testnet only, with code that is days old.
In short
CKB has one lock today built to resist a quantum computer: SPHINCS+. We built a second one, on ML-DSA, another finished NIST standard.
At the same security level it costs about a third as much on chain, and it signs in milliseconds where SPHINCS+ takes about a second.
The price is trust: ML-DSA leans on newer maths than SPHINCS+. It is not safer, and SPHINCS+ stays the careful choice for savings.
We are asking two things: try to break it, and tell us whether CKB wants a second lock at all.
The details a reviewer needs are folded away under each section. Open them to check us.
Why
Most CKB addresses are protected by a kind of signature that a large enough quantum computer could forge. None exists yet, but coins are meant to be held for a long time. CKB already has an answer on mainnet: the SPHINCS+ lock from the Nervos team, which has had an external audit. This post is about whether it should stand alone.
What each scheme asks you to trust
Every signature is safe only as long as some maths problem stays hard. So the first question is which problem.
What each scheme asks you to trust1600×900 61.1 KB
SPHINCS+ needs only a hash function, the same kind of building block CKB already relies on everywhere. Nothing practical assumes less.
ML-DSA needs a hash function and a second problem, about lattices, which is believed hard for quantum computers but has been studied for less time. It assumes more than SPHINCS+, not something separate.
Falcon is not a standard yet, so we measured it and did not build on it.
So ML-DSA is not a safer lock than SPHINCS+. And having two locks does not protect anyone twice: each address depends entirely on the lock it chose. What a second lock gives is a choice, a second implementation, and somewhere to move if one scheme or its code weakens. A lock that needs both signatures would give real protection against either one failing. We did not build that one, and it is the obvious next step if this thread asks for it.
The fine print: standards and security categories
ML-DSA is FIPS 204, final since August 2024, and the scheme NIST named as its primary signature standard. SPHINCS+ is FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA), final the same day, and the one NIST keeps in case lattices fail.
Falcon (FN-DSA) has been selected by NIST, but FIPS 206 is not published.
NIST sorts parameter sets into security categories from 1 to 5. A category is each scheme’s own claim under its own assumption. It does not say which assumption is safer.
The numbers 44, 65 and 87 are ML-DSA’s three parameter sets, at categories 2, 3 and 5. SPHINCS+ has sets at categories 1, 3 and 5.
The curve signature CKB uses by default is ECDSA over secp256k1. Shor’s algorithm recovers its private key from the public key.
What the lock checks
The signature covers the whole transaction, so nothing in it can be changed after signing, and a signature made for one address cannot be reused on another.
One code hash, three levels, the whole transaction signed1600×900 73.6 KB
Exactly what is signed, for script developers
The signature covers the transaction hash (inputs, outputs, cell and header deps), the group’s witnesses and every witness past the inputs, each witness with its length, as the default lock does. Witnesses of other locks’ inputs are covered by those locks.
The lock’s own script hash goes first in the message. A signature made for one deployment or hash type opens no other.
The args are one byte for the level and blake2b-256 of the public key. A key of one level cannot pass under another.
The witness lock field is the public key followed by the signature, exact sizes. Every witness is read in 4 KB pieces, so an oversized witness cannot run the script out of memory.
A cell under it needs 74 CKB at least, for its 33 bytes of args.
How it was checked
We tested it against NIST’s own test cases, against a second library written by someone else, and against thousands of transactions changed after signing. Every one of those was refused. Then we ran the same tests on a lock we broke on purpose, to prove the tests can tell a broken lock from a sound one.
Checked, with controls that must fail1600×900 85.7 KB
Our own attempts to break the lock found no way to spend, replay or reshape a transaction. The same attempts on the wallet side found two bugs, both fixed: the wallet trusted an address stored in the browser without checking it, and a token sent to the account by a stranger blocked it from sending (nothing was lost). None of this is an outside review, which is why we are asking for one.
Each test and its numbers
Against the standard: the 45 ACVP signature verification vectors for the interface the lock uses, run on the CKB-VM build of the verifier. 45 of 45.
Against a second implementation: 600 signatures from an independent JavaScript library and 3,000 altered copies. The lock’s verifier, built for CKB-VM, gave the same verdict on all 3,600.
Against change: 3,000 random signed transactions, then the same 3,000 with one thing changed that the signature covers. All refused.
Against an adversarial engine: our mutation engine bent eight signed payments 2,726 ways (each of the three levels under two hash types, plus two inputs in the group at level 65). None accepted.
Against malformed input: 10,000 random signatures and witnesses, every one refused with the expected code.
On a local dev chain for 45 minutes: 160 transactions committed, and 148 tampered copies sent ahead of the honest one, all refused by the script.
Controls: the transaction runs each have one, a build of the lock with a check switched off that the same run must catch. With no signature check, the engine reports 188 findings and 295 of 300 changed transactions pass.
Where it is on testnet
The code cell on testnet is our build of the repository, byte for byte (same data hash). There are two copies: one pinned by data hash, and one behind a type id whose code cell sits under an ML-DSA-87 key. Anyone using the second copy trusts the holder of that key, which is us; the upgrade we ran rewrote the same code.
Pinned copy: 0xe3c00435…
Upgradable copy: 0xfc80ffd9…
A spend, an upgrade and a spend after it: 0x52523157…, 0xe8a353d3…, 0x1bab570f…
What it does not give you
It is not the safest option. ML-DSA assumes more than SPHINCS+. For coins held for decades, SPHINCS+ remains the careful choice.
The code is new. The lock is days old and the libraries under it are recent.
The wallet is not post-quantum from end to end. The signature on chain is. The passkey that unlocks the key on your phone still uses today’s cryptography.
Lose the passkey, lose the account, unless the wallet gives another way in. Ours does not yet.
One testnet copy can be changed by us. It sits behind a key we hold.
The same limits, for cryptographers
The message is a 32-byte blake2b digest, so collision strength is 2^128 at every level, against someone who can get you to sign a transaction they prepared. That is category 2. The higher levels buy margin against better lattice attacks, not a higher overall category. This is true of any lock on CKB.
The verifier is the fips204 crate, unchanged, in a release three weeks old. The JavaScript library that signs does not claim constant-time execution. Verification on chain handles no secrets; signing in a browser does.
In our wallet branch the seed is the passkey’s PRF output through HKDF-SHA-256, and signing is hedged. The passkey itself, and its sync, rest on classical cryptography.
What the safety costs
Three costs: the computing a node does to check a signature (cycles), the bytes it adds to the chain, and the time a person waits to sign. Each chart compares like with like, at the same NIST category.
Cycles to verify, category by category1600×900 63.1 KB
Bytes on chain: public key and signature1600×900 62.6 KB
Time to sign, in JavaScript on a desktop1600×900 61.8 KB
At the same category, ML-DSA takes about a third of the computing and a third to a quarter of the bytes. That is the whole trade: ML-DSA is cheaper to use, and the price is the extra assumption.
How these were measured
ML-DSA is the full lock, measured on real testnet spends.
The SPHINCS+ figures are from its own README (sha2, C build, whole script).
The secp256k1 and Falcon figures are verification only in a test envelope, so a full lock would cost slightly more.
Signing was timed in Node on one desktop PC, with @noble/post-quantum: median of 200 signatures for ML-DSA, 7 for SPHINCS+. It was not measured on a phone.
SPHINCS+ can also sign fast: its 128f set takes 46 ms, and then costs 32M cycles and a 17 KB signature on chain.
In a wallet
We tried it in a branch of Cellula Wallet, to see what it is like to use. The person sees every input and output before the passkey is asked.
The review before signing780×1688 111 KB
The questions
Would you read the lock and try to break it? The repository has the code, the tests, the controls and the benchmark.
Does CKB want a second post-quantum lock, and in which shape?
SPHINCS+ alone is enough
A second lock, as a choice
Only as a hybrid that needs both signatures
Post-quantum locks are not a priority yet
Not sure
0

Corrections are welcome, above all on the security argument.
